<P style="page-break-before:never; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Share repurchase program</I>. &nbsp;In 2005, we repurchased 5.0 million shares at an average price of $18.98 per share for approximately $94.3 million.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Self-tender offer</I>. &nbsp;In 2005, we repurchased 8.1 million shares at $26.00 per share for approximately $211.0 million.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Amended credit facility</I>. &nbsp;In September 2005, we entered into a new, five-year secured $300 million credit facility. &nbsp;Under our new credit facility, we have increased borrowing capacity for permitted acquisitions, working capital and capital expenditures and other general corporate purposes. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2005, we had borrowings of $93.8 million, $17.0 million in letters of credit outstanding and unused borrowing capacity of $189.2 million under the new credit facility.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10.5pt" align=justify><I>Issuance of senior, secured notes</I>. &nbsp;On October 12, 2005, we entered into a note purchase agreement providing for the issuance and sale of $100 million aggregate principal amount of floating rate, senior secured notes due October 12, 2012.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Warehouse fire in U.K. operations</I>. &nbsp;On January 9, 2005, our London (Thurrock) warehouse and all contents were destroyed by fire. &nbsp;We incurred $1.2 million of operating losses in the first quarter of 2005 as a result of the fire and received an interim payment totaling $928,000 during the second quarter of 2005 on our business interruption claim submitted to our insurance carriers. &nbsp;In addition, we also accrued a liability $823,000 for estimated cargo claims in excess of policy limits and incurred a lease surrender charge of $1.6 million.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Claims activity</I>. &nbsp;We incurred $4.0 million of increased claims activity in the fourth quarter, excluding the warehouse fire in the U.K., for vehicle and workers compensation matters.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Cash flows from operations</I>. &nbsp;Cash flows from operations during the year ended December 31, 2005 were $156.1 million, reflecting improved management of our working capital, particularly through continued focus on our collection of trade receivables.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Global deployment of information technology systems</I>. &nbsp;In 2005, we continued the global deployment of our EGL Vision Suite of Technologies &#150; Logistics Vision, Financial Vision and People Vision. &nbsp;&#147;Logistics Vision&#148; is the freight forwarding system that allows a seamless flow of data across the globe, eliminating duplicate data entry on multiple systems. &nbsp;&#147;Financial Vision&#148; is the Oracle-based financial system that allows global visibility of financial results, streamlined financial reporting and the ability to automate intercompany accounting and settlements. &nbsp;&#147;People Vision&#148; is the Oracle-based human resources application that allows global visibility to employee tracking, training and development. &nbsp;Management continues to believe that successful deployment of systems remains a critical component of improving operational efficiencies and effectively growing the business. &nbsp;The global deployment of EGL Vision will continue into 2006.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We plan in 2006 to work towards continued revenue growth within our existing network and continued improvement of working capital management plus improving yields and operational efficiencies. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt"><BR>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt"><B>Results of Operations</B></P>
<P style="margin:0pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Our principal services are air freight forwarding, ocean freight forwarding, customs brokerage and other value-added logistics services. &nbsp;Revenues for air freight and ocean freight consolidations (indirect shipments) include reimbursements from customers for the cost of transporting such freight. &nbsp;Revenues for air freight and ocean freight agency or direct shipments, customs brokerage and other services, include only the fees or commissions for these services. &nbsp;We believe that a comparison of gross revenues by product best measures the relative importance of our principal services, while a comparison of net revenue margins (net revenues as a percent of gross revenues) best measures the performance of each product line. &nbsp;A comparison of operating expenses as a percent of net revenues considers the relationship between operating expenses and operating revenues. &nbsp;The following table provides certain statement of income data attributable to our principal services during the periods indicated.</P>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:5.5pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>2005 Compared to 2004</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Revenues</I>. &nbsp;Revenues increased $355.1 million, or 13.0%, to $3,096.5 million in 2005, compared to $2,741.4 million in 2004, due to an increase in air freight forwarding revenues of $236.0 million, an increase in ocean freight forwarding revenues of $52.2 million and an increase in customs brokerage and other revenues of $66.8 million. &nbsp;Net revenues, which represent revenues less freight transportation costs, increased $83.1 million, or 9.6%, to $948.5 million in 2005, compared to $865.4 million in 2004. &nbsp;Net revenue margins (net revenues as a percentage of revenues) declined by 100 basis points in 2005 to 30.6%, as compared to 31.6% in 2004. &nbsp;The decrease in margins reflects rising fuel costs and the continued acceleration of growth in international air and ocean products which carry a lower net revenue margin but higher net revenue per shipment. Our international revenues and costs also increased slightly over the prior year due to the effects of translating amounts to the U.S. dollar.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>30</P>
<P style="margin:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<HR style="padding-top:7.2pt; padding-bottom:7.2pt" noshade size=1.333>
<P style="page-break-before:never; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Air freight forwarding revenues</I>. &nbsp;Air freight forwarding revenues increased $236.0 million, or 13.1%, to $2,035.0 million in 2005, compared to $1,799.0 million in 2004, primarily due to continuing volume and shipment increases in Asia Pacific and volume increases in North America.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Air freight forwarding net revenues increased $50.0 million, or 9.8%, to $558.1 million in 2005, compared to $508.1 million in 2004. &nbsp;Air freight forwarding net revenues increased primarily in North America followed by Asia Pacific and Europe/Middle East. &nbsp;The air freight forwarding margin (net revenues as a percentage of revenues) decreased to 27.4% for 2005, as compared to 28.2% for 2004, primarily due to declines in Asia Pacific resulting from the pass through of rising fuel costs to our customers which increased gross revenues without corresponding increases in net revenues. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Ocean freight forwarding revenues</I>. &nbsp;Ocean freight forwarding revenues increased $52.2 million, or 13.3%, to $443.8 million in 2005, compared to $391.6 million in 2004 primarily due to volume increases in Asia Pacific, Europe/Middle East and North America due to our increased focus on the ocean market and our customers&#146; continued shift toward a lower cost deferred product.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Ocean freight forwarding net revenues increased $13.7 million, or 18.0%, to $89.9 million in 2005, compared to $76.2 million in 2004, while the ocean freight forwarding margin increased to 20.3% for 2005, compared to 19.5% for 2004. &nbsp;Ocean freight forwarding margins steadily declined throughout 2004 due to higher carrier rates and increased volumes of business in the competitive transpacific east-bound and Asia to Europe tradelanes. &nbsp;Margins have begun to increase in 2005 from improved margins on ocean exports out of North America due to more available capacity introduced by ocean carriers.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Customs brokerage and other revenues</I>. &nbsp;Customs brokerage and other revenues, which include imports, warehousing, distribution and other logistics services, increased $66.8 million, or 12.1%, to $617.7 million in 2005, compared to $550.9 million in 2004. &nbsp;Customs brokerage revenues increased primarily due to growth in Europe/Middle East and North America trade activity. &nbsp;Warehousing and logistics revenues increased due to growth in all geographic divisions. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Customs brokerage and other net revenues increased $19.4 million, or 6.9%, to $300.4 million in 2005, compared to $281.0 million in 2004. &nbsp;Customs brokerage and other margins, however, decreased to 48.6% for 2005, compared to 51.0% for 2004 primarily due to lower margins in Europe/Middle East and North America resulting from termination or completion of several high margin logistics projects.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:9.65pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:12.5pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Personnel costs</I>. &nbsp;Personnel costs include all compensation expenses, including those relating to sales commissions, incentive programs and salaries and to headquarters employees and executive officers. &nbsp;Personnel costs increased $40.7 million, or 8.5%, to $522.0 million in 2005, compared to $481.3 million in 2004. &nbsp;The increase in personnel costs was due primarily to increased hiring as a result of the increase in business activity and salary adjustments. &nbsp;In addition, during the year ended December 31, 2005, we recorded charges of $1.6 million for workforce reductions, mainly in certain European and U.S. locations. &nbsp;We have historically maintained incentive bonus, profit sharing and sales commission compensation plans to reward attainment of targets. &nbsp;Our incentive bonus and profit sharing compensation plans include a combination of target achievements related to total company financial performance, business unit financial performance and individual goals and objectives. &nbsp;For 2005, more challenging financial performance targets were introduced which have resulted in a lower level of incentive compensation expense in 2005. &nbsp;As a percentage of net revenues, personnel costs decreased to 55.0% in 2005, compared to 55.6% in 2004. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:9.65pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:12.5pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Other selling, general and administrative expenses. &nbsp;</I>Other selling, general and administrative expenses increased $34.3 million, or 11.3%, to $337.0 million in 2005, compared to $302.7 million in 2004. &nbsp;As a percentage of net revenues, other selling, general and administrative expenses were 35.5% in 2005, compared to 35.0% in 2004. &nbsp;The increase is due primarily to the $2.9 million penalty for improper government billings, increased fees for the continued deployment of our Vision suite of technologies &#150; freight forwarding, accounting and human resources systems &#150; as well as increased accounting and tax </P>
<P style="margin-top:4.6pt; margin-bottom:9.65pt; line-height:12.5pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>31</P>
<P style="margin:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<HR style="padding-top:7.2pt; padding-bottom:7.2pt" noshade size=1.333>
<P style="page-break-before:never; margin-top:4.6pt; margin-bottom:9.65pt; line-height:12.5pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:4.6pt; margin-bottom:9.65pt; line-height:12.5pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>fees and increased insurance costs due to higher claims activity in the U.S. and cargo claims accruals relating to the warehouse fire in the U.K.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>EEOC legal settlement</I>. &nbsp;During 2005, we recaptured $6.0 million of the $8.5 million previously held in a fund to resolve potential claims in connection with a 2001 consent decree with the EEOC, resulting primarily from a significantly lower number of qualified claimants than originally projected.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Nonoperating income (expense), net.</I> &nbsp;Nonoperating income (expense), net includes interest expense, interest income, minority interest expense, equity in earnings (losses) from affiliates, foreign exchange gains (losses) and other nonoperating income (expenses). &nbsp;Nonoperating income was $5.1 million in 2005 as compared to nonoperating income of $7.3 million in 2004. &nbsp;In 2005, we had foreign exchange gains of $2.5 million, as compared to foreign exchange losses of $1.4 million in 2004. &nbsp;In 2004, we sold our investment in Miami Air and realized a gain of approximately $6.7 million. &nbsp;We sold our investment in TDS in 2004 for approximately $51.4 million in cash. &nbsp;We received approximately $45.3 million of the sale proceeds in August 2004. &nbsp;In 2004, the TDS sale resulted in a gain of approximately $5.9 million, which excludes the proceeds held in escrow. &nbsp;In 2005, we recorded a gain of $4.0 million following the resolution of certain contingencies. &nbsp;See note 6 of the notes to our consolidated financial statements. &nbsp;Additionally, we incurred interest expense, net of $2.7 million in 2005, compared to $6.2 million in 2004, and had equity losses of affiliates of $85,000 in 2005, compared to earnings of $1.7 million in 2004.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Effective tax rate.</I> &nbsp;Our effective tax rate for 2005 was 42.2% compared to 42.6% for 2004. &nbsp;Our effective tax rates fluctuate due to changes in the level of pre-tax income in foreign countries that have different rates and certain income and/or expenses that are permanently non-taxable or non-deductible in certain jurisdictions including the U.S. &nbsp;The penalty related to the KBR war surcharge is non-deductible for U.S. tax purposes.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>2004 Compared to 2003</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Revenues</I>. &nbsp;Revenues increased $598.0 million, or 27.9%, to $2,741.4 million in 2004, compared to $2,143.4 million in 2003, primarily due to an increase in air freight forwarding revenues of $389.3 million, an increase in ocean freight forwarding revenues of $101.1 million and an increase in customs brokerage and other revenues of $107.7 million. &nbsp;Net revenues, which represent revenues less freight transportation costs, increased $130.1 million, or 17.7%, to $865.4 million in 2004, compared to $735.3 million in 2003. &nbsp;Net revenue margins (net revenues as a percentage of revenues) declined by 270 basis points in 2004 to 31.6%, as compared to 34.3% in 2003. &nbsp;The decrease in margins reflects (i) higher transportation and fuel costs due to capacity constraints, mainly from Asia; (ii) fuel surcharges absorbed by the business; (iii) an acceleration of growth in international air and ocean products which carry a lower net revenue margin but higher net revenue per shipment; and (iv) pass-through of certain fuel and security surcharges, which increased gross revenues without corresponding increases in net revenues. &nbsp;Our international revenues and costs also increased slightly over the prior year due to the effects of translating amounts to the U.S. dollar.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Air freight forwarding revenues</I>. &nbsp;Air freight forwarding revenues increased $389.3 million, or 27.6%, to $1,799.0 million in 2004, compared to $1,409.7 million in 2003 due to volume increases in all geographic divisions, particularly Asia Pacific, North America and Europe/Middle East. &nbsp;This growth is primarily from improvements in shipment volumes and international charter activity.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Air freight forwarding net revenues increased $82.1 million, or 19.3%, to $508.1 million in 2004, compared to $426.0 million in 2003. &nbsp;Air freight forwarding net revenues increased primarily in North America followed by Europe/Middle East and Asia Pacific. &nbsp;The air freight forwarding margin (net revenues as a percentage of revenues) decreased to 28.2% for 2004, as compared to 30.2% for 2003 primarily due to declines in North America and Asia Pacific resulting from higher volume levels in certain trade lanes that carry a lower margin, higher fuel surcharges from carriers and increases in international charter activity which typically carries a lower margin. &nbsp;These decreases were offset by </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>32</P>
<P style="margin:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>

<P style="page-break-before:never; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>increases in air freight forwarding margins in Europe/Middle East primarily due to an increase in higher margin direct air shipments relative to consolidated shipments.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Ocean freight forwarding revenues</I>. &nbsp;Ocean freight forwarding revenues increased $101.1 million, or 34.8%, to $391.6 million in 2004, compared to $290.5 million in 2003. &nbsp;The increase in revenues was principally due to volume increases in all geographic divisions due to our increased focus on the ocean market and our customers&#146; continued shift toward a lower cost deferred product.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Ocean freight forwarding net revenues increased $12.3 million, or 19.2%, to $76.2 million in 2004, compared to $63.9 million in 2003 while the ocean freight forwarding margin decreased to 19.5% for 2004, compared to 22.0% for 2003. &nbsp;The ocean freight forwarding margins decreased due to continued rising transportation costs and shipping capacity constraints, particularly between Asia and North America.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Customs brokerage and other revenues</I>. &nbsp;Customs brokerage and other revenues, which include imports, warehousing, distribution and other logistics services, increased $107.7 million, or 24.3%, to $550.9 million in 2004, compared to $443.2 million in 2003. &nbsp;Customs brokerage revenues increased in 2004, compared to 2003 due to growth in Europe/Middle East trade activity and U.S. imports. &nbsp;The increase is also due to higher warehousing, distribution and other logistics revenues resulting from multiple new logistics projects in North America and a $2.8 million termination fee for a logistics project in Europe.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Customs brokerage and other net revenues increased $35.6 million, or 14.5%, to $281.0 million in 2004, compared to $245.4 million in 2003. &nbsp;Customs brokerage and other margins, however, decreased to 51.0% for 2004, compared to 55.4% for 2003 primarily due to lower margins in Europe/Middle East, Asia Pacific and North America resulting from termination or completion of several higher margin projects.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Personnel costs</I>. &nbsp;Personnel costs include all compensation expenses, including those relating to sales commissions and salaries and to headquarters employees and executive officers. &nbsp;Personnel costs increased $59.3 million, or 14.1%, to $481.3 million in 2004, compared to $422.0 million in 2003. &nbsp;As a percentage of net revenues, personnel costs were 55.6% in 2004, compared to 57.4% in 2003. &nbsp;The increase in personnel costs was primarily due to the increase in business activity and foreign exchange translation effects.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Other selling, general and administrative expenses</I>. &nbsp;Other selling, general and administrative expenses increased $32.8 million, or 12.2%, to $302.7 million in 2004, compared to $269.9 million in 2003. &nbsp;As a percentage of net revenues, other selling, general and administrative expenses were 35.0% in 2004, compared to 36.7% in 2003. &nbsp;The increase in other selling, general and administrative expenses is primarily due to an increase in facility expense. &nbsp;The increase is mainly associated with additional or larger replacement facilities to accommodate increased operations. &nbsp;A portion of the increase in facility expense is due to a $3.8 million net increase in facility accruals mainly covering North America. &nbsp;In North America, we consolidated three facilities into our new facility in Miami, which was completed in late 2003. &nbsp;We subleased one of the North American facilities for less than our remaining obligation and accrued the net amount of lease payments we expect to pay over the remaining lease term. &nbsp;During the year, we accrued additional lease expense in North America and Europe on two vacant facilities due to unfavorable market conditions near the facilities. We subsequently released these accruals as we decided to utilize the North America facility for increased operations and the facility in Europe was subleased earlier than assumed in the previous accrual. &nbsp;We also released a $1.6 million accrual originally recorded in prior years for a facility in Houston, Texas as we decided to utilize this facility for increased operations. Other selling, general and administrative expenses have also increased due to higher professional fees and communications costs related to systems implementations and preparations for internal controls testing required by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 and foreign exchange effects.</P>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Nonoperating income (expense), net.</I> &nbsp;Nonoperating income (expense), net includes interest expense, interest income, minority interest expense, equity in earnings (losses) from affiliates, foreign exchange gains (losses) and other nonoperating income (expenses). &nbsp;Nonoperating income, net was $7.3 million in 2004, as compared to nonoperating expense of $6.2 million in 2003. &nbsp;In 2004, we sold our investment in Miami Air and realized a gain of approximately $6.7 million. &nbsp;We had previously written off our investment in Miami Air in 2002. &nbsp;We sold our investment in TDS Logistics, Inc. (TDS) in 2004 for approximately $51.4 million in cash. &nbsp;We received approximately $45.3 million of the sale proceeds in August 2004 and an additional $557,000 in January 2005. &nbsp;The remaining $5.5 million of the TDS sale proceeds are being held in escrow subject to the resolution of certain contingencies and time periods. &nbsp;The TDS sale resulted in a gain of approximately $5.9 million, which excludes the proceeds held in escrow. &nbsp;See note 6 of the notes to our consolidated financial statements. &nbsp;Additionally, we incurred interest expense, net of $6.2 million in 2004, compared to $4.9 million in 2003, and had equity earnings of affiliates of $1.7 million in 2004, compared to losses of $199,000 in 2003.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Effective tax rate.</I> &nbsp;Our effective tax rate for 2004 was 42.6% compared to 37.8% for 2003. &nbsp;The effective tax rate was higher than 2003 mainly related to additional deferred income tax expense on foreign operations for which additional tax reserves were recorded, as well as lower than expected earnings from certain European countries. &nbsp;Our effective tax rates fluctuate due to changes in the level of pre-tax income in foreign countries that have different rates and certain income and/or expenses that are permanently non-taxable or non-deductible in certain jurisdictions.</P>
<A NAME="_Toc512306403"></A><P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt"><B>Liquidity and Capital Resources</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>General</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Our ability to satisfy our debt obligations, fund working capital and make capital expenditures depends upon our future performance, which is subject to general economic conditions and other factors, some of which are beyond our control. &nbsp;If we achieve significant near-term revenue growth, we may experience a need for increased working capital financing as a result of the difference between our cash collection cycles and the timing of our payments to vendors. &nbsp;Historically we have generated cash flow from operations in the first half of the year higher than in the second half of the year reflecting the seasonality of our business.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We make significant disbursements on behalf of our customers for transportation costs (primarily ocean) and customs duties for which the customer is the primary obligor. &nbsp;The billings to customers for these disbursements, which are several times the amount of revenues and fees derived from these transactions, are not recorded as revenues and expenses on our statement of income; rather, they are reflected in our trade receivables and trade payables. &nbsp;Growth in the level of this activity or lengthening of the period of time between incurring these costs and being reimbursed by our customers for these costs may negatively affect our liquidity.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>As primarily a non-asset based freight forwarder, we do not have the same level of capital expenditures that would be required of an asset based forwarder. &nbsp;We believe our anticipated capital expenditures for 2006 will be in the range of $45 to $50 million, including approximately $32 to $37 million expected on information systems expenditures. &nbsp;Based on current plans, we believe that our existing capital resources, including $111.5 million of cash and cash equivalents and $189.2 million of available borrowing capacity on our credit facility, will be sufficient to meet working capital requirements through December 31, 2006. &nbsp;However, future changes in our business could cause us to consume available resources before that time. &nbsp;Additionally, funds may not be available when needed and even if available, additional funds may be raised through financing arrangements and/or the issuance of preferred </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>34</P>

<BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>or common stock or convertible securities on terms and prices significantly more favorable than those of the currently outstanding common stock, which could have the effect of diluting or adversely affecting the holdings or rights of our existing stockholders. &nbsp;If adequate funds are unavailable, we may be required to delay, scale back or eliminate some of our operating activities, including, without limitation, the timing and extent of our marketing programs, and the extent and timing of hiring additional personnel. &nbsp;We cannot provide assurance that additional financing will be available to us on acceptable terms, or at all.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>2005 Compared to 2004</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Net cash provided by operating activities</I>. &nbsp;Net cash provided by operating activities was $156.1 million in 2005, compared to $32.1 million in 2004. &nbsp;The increase in 2005 was primarily due to an increase in net income and a $49.4 million net increase in cash from changes in working capital for 2005, compared to $61.4 million net decrease for 2004. &nbsp;The increase in cash from changes in working capital is due to a $20.2 million decrease in trade receivables due to improved collection efforts as evidenced by a 13% decrease in days sales outstanding from 70 days at December 31, 2004 to 61 days at December 31, 2005. &nbsp;In addition to the decrease in trade receivables, there was a $29.5 million increase in payables and other accrued liabilities, compared with a $79.8 million increase in 2004.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Net cash used in investing activitie</I>s. &nbsp;Net cash used in investing activities in 2005 was $29.4 million, compared to $7.0 million in 2004. &nbsp;Capital expenditures were $41.2 million during 2005, compared to $38.2 million during 2004, a $3.0 million increase. &nbsp;The expenditures in 2005 were mainly due to the implementation of our operational and financial systems, other software expenditures and equipment purchases. &nbsp;$12.5 million of the capital expenditures in 2005 relate to the purchase of a corporate plane. &nbsp;Restricted cash decreased by $5.3 million in 2005 as compared to an increase of $3.4 million in 2004. &nbsp;During 2005 and 2004, in connection with our acquisition of Miami International Forwarders in 2003 and the buyout of a minority interest partner in Thailand in 2001, we made earnout payments totaling $4.4 million and $3.3 million, respectively. &nbsp;During 2004, we received proceeds of $6.7 million for the sale of our interest in an unconsolidated affiliate, Miami Air, to an unrelated party and proceeds of $45.3 million for the sale of our interest in an unconsolidated affiliate, TDS, to an unrelated party. &nbsp;During the second quarter of 2004, we acquired the outside ownership of our consolidated affiliates in France, Spain and Portugal for aggregate consideration of $16.2 million in cash. &nbsp;In 2005 and 2004, we received proceeds of $4.3 million and $1.1 million, respectively, from sales of other property and equipment.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Net cash used in financing activities</I>. &nbsp;Net cash used in financing activities in 2005 was $107.7 million, compared to $22.6 million in 2004. &nbsp;The cash used in financing activities in 2005 consists of $309.3 million in repayments of debt, $211.0 million in cash payments for the repurchase of 8.1 million shares of our outstanding common stock from our tender offer, $94.3 million in cash payments for the repurchase of 5.0 million shares of our outstanding common stock, $3.5 million in payments of financing fees related to our new Amended and Restated Credit Facility, $3.4 million of repayment of financed insurance premiums, $2.7 million from the repayment of short-term debt, net of issuances and $2.2 million in payments of capital lease obligations, offset by $495.6 million in proceeds from the issuance of debt, $21.2 million in proceeds from the exercise of 1.0 million stock options and $1.1 million in proceeds from the issuance of 66,000 shares of common stock from our Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP). &nbsp;The cash used in financing activities in 2004 consists of $6.4 million of repayment of financed insurance premiums, $59.1 million in cash payments for the repurchase of 3.4 million shares of our outstanding common stock, $218.8 million in repayments of debt and $1.1 million in payments of financing fees related to our new Credit Facility, offset by $39.9 million in proceeds from the exercise of 2.1 million stock options, $211.0 million proceeds from the issuance of debt and $791,000 in proceeds from the issuance of 42,000 shares of common stock from our ESPP.</P>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>2004 Compared to 2003</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Net cash provided by operating activities</I>. &nbsp;Net cash provided by operating activities was $32.1 million in 2004, compared to $39.0 million in 2003. &nbsp;The decrease in 2004 was primarily due to a $61.4 million net decrease in cash from changes in working capital for 2004, compared to $30.0 million net decrease for 2003, offset by an increase in net income. &nbsp;The decrease in cash from changes in working capital is due to a significant increase in gross revenues during the month of December 2004, compared to December 2003, resulting in an increase in trade receivables and a 4% increase in days sales outstanding from 67 days at December 31, 2003 to 70 days at December 31, 2004. &nbsp;The increase in trade receivables was offset by an increase in payables and other accrued liabilities.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Net cash used in investing activities</I>. &nbsp;Net cash used in investing activities in 2004 was $7.0 million compared to $49.8 million in 2003. &nbsp;Capital expenditures were $38.2 million during 2004, compared to $26.0 million during 2003, a $12.2 million increase. &nbsp;The expenditures in 2004 were mainly due to the implementation of our operational and financial systems, other software expenditures and equipment purchases. &nbsp;During 2004, we received proceeds of $6.7 million for the sale of our interest in an unconsolidated affiliate, Miami Air, to an unrelated party and proceeds of $45.3 million for the sale of our interest in an unconsolidated affiliate, TDS, to an unrelated party.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>During the second quarter of 2004, we acquired the outside ownership of our consolidated affiliates in France, Spain and Portugal for aggregate consideration of $16.2 million in cash. &nbsp;During the same period, we also made a $3.2 million earnout payment to the former owners of MIF due to achievement of post-acquisition performance criteria specified in the April 2003 purchase and sale agreement. &nbsp;During the second quarter of 2003, we completed several acquisitions with aggregate cash consideration of $21.1 million. &nbsp;In April 2003, we acquired MIF for $13.7 million in cash and we purchased from one of our joint venture partners a 26% interest in our operating subsidiary in Singapore for approximately $5.7 million in cash. &nbsp;In 2003, we also completed an acquisition of an international freight forwarder and customs broker in France for approximately $1.1 million, net of cash acquired and made a $600,000 earnout payment related to an acquisition completed in a prior year.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>During 2004 and 2003, we received proceeds of $1.1 million and $4.2 million, respectively, from sales of property and equipment and a sale-lease back transaction.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Net cash used in financing activities</I>. &nbsp;Net cash used in financing activities in 2004 was $22.6 million, compared to $4.8 million in 2003. &nbsp;The cash used in financing activities in 2004 consists of $6.4 million in repayment of financed insurance premiums, $59.1 million in cash payments for the repurchase of 3.4 million shares of our outstanding common stock, $218.8 million in repayments of debt and $1.1 million in payments of financing fees related to our new Credit Facility, offset by $39.9 million in proceeds from the exercise of 2.1 million stock options, $211.0 million in proceeds from the issuance of debt and $791,000 in proceeds from the issuance of 42,000 shares of common stock from our ESPP. &nbsp;Cash used in financing activities in 2003 consisted of $9.1 million for repayment of financed insurance premiums and $214,000 in cash payments to our minority interest partners, offset by $4.1 million in proceeds from the exercise of 324,000 stock options and $540,000 in proceeds from the issuance of 43,000 shares of common stock from our ESPP.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Other factors affecting our liquidity and capital resources</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Amended and Restated Credit Agreement. </I>&nbsp;We entered into an agreement dated as of September 30, 2005 establishing a $300 million, senior secured revolving credit facility (the Amended and Restated Credit Agreement). &nbsp;The Amended and Restated Credit Agreement amends and restates our prior revolving credit agreement dated as of September 15, 2004, as previously amended (the Prior Credit Agreement). &nbsp;The Amended and Restated Credit Agreement is with a syndicate of 13 financial institutions with Bank of America, N.A., as lender and administrative agent and matures on September 30, 2010. &nbsp;</P>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Loans under the Amended and Restated Credit Agreement will bear interest initially at a rate per annum equal to either, at our option, (1) LIBOR plus 1.25% or (2) the Base Rate (defined as the higher of Bank of America, N.A.&#146;s prime rate or 0.50% over the Federal Funds rate). &nbsp;In addition, we are required to pay a commitment fee of 0.30% on the undrawn amounts under the Amended and Restated Credit Agreement. &nbsp;Interest rates and commitment fees under the Amended and Restated Credit Agreement are subject to increase or decrease as a function of the ratio of our Consolidated Net Funded Indebtedness to Consolidated EBITDA (each as defined in the Amended and Restated Credit Agreement). &nbsp;We may select interest periods of one, two, three or six months for LIBOR loans, subject to availability. &nbsp;Interest will be payable at the end of the selected interest period, but no less frequently than quarterly.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Under the Amended and Restated Credit Agreement, we are subject to various covenants, including, among others, the following:</P>

<P style="margin:0pt; padding-left:36pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The Note Purchase Agreement contains customary events of default. &nbsp;If a default occurs and is continuing, the Notes then outstanding shall (either automatically or by declaration of the holders of more than 50% of the principal amount of Notes then outstanding, depending upon the circumstances resulting in the default) become immediately due and payable. &nbsp;If an event of default occurs and is continuing because we failed to pay principal, interest or other amounts due and payable on the Notes, then any Note holder may declare all of the Notes held by it to be immediately due and payable.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Release of restricted cash.</I> &nbsp;In February 2005, in response to a joint motion filed by EGL and the EEOC, a U.S. District Court ordered the return of $6.0 million to us of $8.5 million previously held in an established fund to resolve potential claims in connection with a 2001 consent decree (see note 15 of the notes to our consolidated financial statements). &nbsp;The joint motion and subsequent order resulted in $6.0 million in income in the first quarter of 2005.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Capital expenditures</I>. &nbsp;We are in the process of developing and implementing computer system solutions for operational, human resources and financial systems. &nbsp;Our capital expenditures were approximately $10.1 million and $18.5 million related to the development of these systems during 2005 and 2004, respectively. &nbsp;Our expected capital expenditures for 2006 are approximately $45 to $50 million, including approximately $32 to $37 million for information technology development and upgrades.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>TDS Logistics, Inc</I>. &nbsp;In August 2004, we sold our investment in TDS Logistics, Inc. (TDS) to an unrelated party for approximately $51.4 million in cash. &nbsp;We received approximately $45.3 million of the sale proceeds in August 2004, with additional payments totaling $3.3 million in 2005 and $1.3 million in January 2006. &nbsp;The remaining $1.5 million of the sale proceeds are held in escrow subject to the resolution of certain contingencies and time periods. &nbsp;The sale resulted in an initial gain of $5.9 million in 2004 and an additional gain of $4.0 million in 2005 when certain funds were released out of escrow. &nbsp;These amounts are included in non-operating income in our consolidated statement of income.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Share repurchase program</I>. &nbsp;On April 4, 2005, our Board of Directors adopted a stock repurchase program to repurchase up to $60 million in value of our outstanding common stock depending on market conditions and other factors with an expiration date of August 4, 2005. &nbsp;On May 31, 2005, the Board of Directors approved an increase in the maximum dollar amount of shares to be repurchased from $60 million to $120 million and extended the expiration date to September 28, 2005. &nbsp;As of September 28, 2005, we had repurchased a total of 5.0 million shares at an average price of $18.98 per share for approximately $94.3 million.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>On August 29, 2005, the Board of Directors authorized a modified &#147;Dutch Auction&#148; self-tender offer to purchase up to 9,615,000 shares (up to $250 million) of its common stock, representing approximately 20% of its approximately 47.2 million outstanding shares as of August 24, 2005. &nbsp;The tender offer commenced on Tuesday, August 30, 2005 and expired on Wednesday, September 28, 2005. &nbsp;In the tender offer, shareholders had the opportunity to tender some or all of their shares at a price not less than $22.50 per share or more than $26.00 per share, net to the seller in cash, without interest.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>On October 4, 2005, we announced the final results of the tender offer. &nbsp;An aggregate of 8,085,958 shares were properly tendered and not withdrawn at or below a price of $26.00. &nbsp;Because shareholders tendered less than 9,615,000 shares, there was no proration of tendered shares. &nbsp;We financed the tender offer with the use of cash on hand and borrowings of $196.0 million under both the new $300.0 </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>39</P>
<P style="margin:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>

<P style="page-break-before:never; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>million line of credit facility and the $100.0 million bridge loan that was refinanced by the issuance of $100.0 million of floating rate senior secured notes due in October 2012 (see note 8 of the notes to our consolidated financial statements). &nbsp;As a result, we accepted for purchase and paid approximately $211.0 million for all 8,085,958 shares at a price of $26.00 per share. &nbsp;Any shares received in the tender offer that were not tendered properly were returned to the tendering shareholders. &nbsp;The shares purchased pursuant to the tender offer represented approximately 17.1% of EGL&#146;s outstanding shares as of September 30, 2005.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>In February and March 2004, our Board of Directors authorized the repurchase of up to $65 million in value of our outstanding common stock depending on market conditions and other factors. &nbsp;During the program, which expired in July 2004, we repurchased approximately 3.4 million shares of our common stock at an average price of $17.37 per share for approximately $59.1 million.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Stock options</I>. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2005, we had outstanding non-qualified stock options to purchase an aggregate of 3.1 million shares of common stock at exercise prices equal to the fair market value of the underlying common stock on the dates of grant (prices ranging from $8.88 to $37.29). &nbsp;At the time a non-qualified stock option is exercised, we will generally be entitled to a deduction for federal and state income tax purposes equal to the difference between the fair market value of the common stock on the date of exercise and the option price. &nbsp;As a result of non-qualified stock option exercises in 2005 and 2004 to purchase an aggregate of 1.0 million and 2.1 million shares of common stock, we are entitled to a federal and state income tax deduction of approximately $12.1 million and $19.2 million, respectively. &nbsp;We have recognized a reduction of our federal and state income tax obligations of approximately $5.0 million and $7.8 million in 2005 and 2004, respectively. &nbsp;Accordingly, we recorded an increase to additional paid-in capital and a reduction to current taxes payable. &nbsp;Any exercises of non-qualified stock options in the future at exercise prices below the then fair market value of the common stock may also result in tax deductions equal to the difference between those amounts. &nbsp;There is uncertainty as to whether the exercises will occur, the amount of any deductions, and our ability to fully utilize any tax deductions.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:-13pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Off-Balance Sheet Arrangements</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:180pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I><BR></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>As is common in our industry, we have entered into certain off-balance sheet arrangements in the ordinary course of business that result in risks not directly reflected in our balance sheets. &nbsp;Our significant off-balance sheet arrangements include liabilities associated with guarantees secured by letters of credit, surety bonds and security time deposits and non-cancelable operating leases. &nbsp;We have not engaged in any off-balance sheet financing arrangements through special purpose entities.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Guarantees.</I> &nbsp;We guarantee certain financial liabilities, the majority of which relate to our freight forwarding operations. &nbsp;In the normal course of our business, we are required to guarantee certain amounts related to customs bonds and services received from airlines. &nbsp;These types of guarantees are usual and customary in the freight forwarding industry. &nbsp;We operate as a customs broker and prepare and file all formal documentation required for clearance through customs agencies, obtain customs bonds, facilitate the payment of import duties on behalf of the importer and arrange for payment of collect freight charges. &nbsp;We also assist the importer in obtaining the most advantageous commodity classifications, qualifying for duty drawback refunds and arranges for surety bonds for importers.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We secure these guarantees primarily by three methods: &nbsp;a $75 million standby letter of credit sub-facility included within our Amended and Restated Credit Agreement, surety bonds and security time deposits. &nbsp;Security time deposits are restricted as to withdrawal for a specified timeframe and are classified on our balance sheet as restricted cash. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2005, we had $17.0 million in letters of credit outstanding. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We also issue IATA (International Air Transportation Association) related guarantees, customs bonds and other working capital credit line guarantees in the normal course of business. &nbsp;IATA related guarantees and customs bonds are issued to facilitate the movement and clearance of freight. &nbsp;Working capital credit line guarantees include, but are not limited to, guarantees associated with insurance </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>40</P>
<P style="margin:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<HR style="padding-top:7.2pt; padding-bottom:7.2pt" noshade size=1.333>
<P style="page-break-before:never; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>requirements and certain potential tax obligations. &nbsp;Generally, guarantees have one-year or two-year terms and are renewed upon expiration. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2005, total IATA related guarantees, customs bonds and other working capital credit line guarantees were approximately $85.4 million. &nbsp;Approximately $52.4 million of guarantees, customs bonds and borrowings against credit line guarantees were outstanding, including guarantees of our trade payables and accrued transportation costs and borrowings against our international credit facilities of $13.4 million, which were recorded as liabilities on our consolidated balance sheet.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Leases.</I> &nbsp;We enter into operating lease agreements, principally for freight operation facilities and office space. &nbsp;These leases are non-cancelable and expire on various dates through 2025. &nbsp;Certain of &nbsp;our lease agreements contain renewal options and rent escalation clauses. &nbsp;These leases allow us to conserve cash by paying a monthly lease payment for use of facilities, rather than purchasing the facilities. &nbsp;Rent expense for operating leases was $80.8 million, $86.9 million and $77.5 million for the years ended December 31, 2005, 2004 and 2003, respectively, which is net of sublease income of $3.7 million, $4.5 million and $3.6 million, respectively. &nbsp;Please refer to Note 16 to our consolidated financial statements for more details regarding our outstanding leases. &nbsp;</P>

<A NAME="_Toc507937533"></A><A NAME="_Toc507937729"></A><A NAME="_Toc507937912"></A><A NAME="_Toc510516214"></A><A NAME="_Toc512306405"></A><P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt"><B>Seasonality</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Historically, our operating results have been subject to a limited degree to seasonal trends when measured on a quarterly basis. &nbsp;Typically, our first fiscal quarter is weaker when compared to our other fiscal quarters of the corresponding year. &nbsp;The seasonality of our business is a result of a variety of factors, including holiday seasons, consumer demand, economic conditions and other factors beyond our control. &nbsp;We cannot accurately forecast many of these factors, nor can we estimate accurately the relative influence of any particular factor. &nbsp;As a result, there can be no assurance that historical patterns, if any, will continue in future periods.</P>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt"><B>Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Use of estimates</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The preparation of financial statements in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles requires management to make estimates that affect the amounts reported in the financial statements and accompanying notes. &nbsp;Management considers many factors in selecting appropriate operational and financial accounting policies and controls, and in developing the assumptions that are used in the preparation of these financial statements. &nbsp;Management must apply significant judgment in this process. &nbsp;Among the factors, but not fully inclusive of all factors that may be considered by management in these processes are:</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:-13pt; padding-left:54pt; text-indent:-18pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>-</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; padding-left:54pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>the range of accounting policies permitted by accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:-13pt; padding-left:54pt; text-indent:-18pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>-</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; padding-left:54pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>management&#146;s understanding of the company&#146;s business &#150; both historical results and expected future results;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:-13pt; padding-left:54pt; text-indent:-18pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>-</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; padding-left:54pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>expectations of the future performance of the economy &#150; domestically, globally and within various sectors that serve our principal customers and suppliers of goods and services;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:-13pt; padding-left:54pt; text-indent:-18pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>-</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; padding-left:54pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>expected rates of change, sensitivity and volatility associated with the assumptions used in developing estimates; and</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:-13pt; padding-left:54pt; text-indent:-18pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>-</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; padding-left:54pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>whether historical trends are expected to be representative of future trends.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The estimation process often times may yield a range of potentially reasonable estimates of the ultimate future outcomes and management must select an amount that lies within that range of reasonable estimates &#150; which may result in the selection of estimates that may be viewed as conservative or aggressive by others &#150; based upon the quantity, quality and risks associated with the variability that might be expected from the future outcome and the factors considered in developing the estimate. &nbsp;Management attempts to use its business and financial accounting judgment in selecting the most appropriate estimate, however, actual amounts could and will differ from those estimates.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Revenue recognition</I></P>
<P style="margin:0pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Domestic revenues and most domestic operating costs are recognized when shipments are picked up from the customer. &nbsp;International revenues and freight consolidation costs are recognized in the period when shipments are tendered to a carrier for transport to a foreign destination. &nbsp;This is one of the permissible methods under Emerging Issues Task Force (EITF) Issue No. 91-9, &#147;Revenue and Expense Recognition for Freight Services in Process.&#148; &nbsp;This method generally results in recognition of revenues and gross profit earlier than methods that do not recognize revenues until a proof of delivery is received. &nbsp;This method of revenue and cost recognition does not result in a material difference than if revenues and costs were recognized upon delivery. &nbsp;Customs brokerage and other revenues are recognized upon completing the documents necessary for customs clearance or completing other fee-based services. &nbsp;Revenues recognized as an indirect air carrier or an ocean freight consolidator include the direct carrier&#146;s charges to EGL for carrying the shipment. &nbsp;Revenues recognized in other capacities include only the commissions and fees received. &nbsp;We report the costs of certain reimbursed incidental activities on a gross basis in revenues and cost of transportation.</P>
<P style="margin:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We derive our revenues from three principal sources: &nbsp;air freight forwarding, ocean freight forwarding, and customs brokerage, import and logistics services.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>43</P>
<P style="margin:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<HR style="padding-top:7.2pt; padding-bottom:7.2pt" noshade size=1.333>
<P style="page-break-before:never; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Air and ocean freight forwarding</I>. &nbsp;As primarily a non-asset based carrier, we do not own transportation assets. &nbsp;Instead, we generate the majority of our air and ocean freight revenues by purchasing transportation services from direct (asset-based) carriers and reselling those services to our customers as an indirect carrier. &nbsp;Additionally, we generate air freight and ocean freight forwarding revenues to a lesser extent as an authorized cargo sales agent.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>As an indirect carrier, we obtain shipments from our customers, consolidate shipments bound for a particular destination, determine the routing, select the direct carrier and tender each consolidated lot as a single shipment to the direct carrier for transportation to a distribution point. &nbsp;We issue a House Airway Bill (HAWB) or a House Ocean Bill of Lading (HOBL) to customers as the contract of carriage. &nbsp;In turn, when the freight is physically tendered to a direct carrier, we receive a contract of carriage known as a Master Airway Bill for air freight shipments and a Master Ocean Bill of Lading for ocean shipments. &nbsp;We are the direct point of contact for service fulfillment and resolving any service failures or claims for lost or damaged freight resulting from either our or the direct carriers&#146; actions. &nbsp;In addition, if we do not collect from our customers, we are still responsible for paying the direct carrier.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Due to the high volume of freight we manage, we generally obtain lower rates from the direct carriers than the rates we charge our customers for individual shipments. &nbsp;This rate differential is the primary source of our air and ocean freight net revenues. &nbsp;We have complete discretion in selecting the means, route and procedures to be followed in the handling, transportation and delivery of freight. &nbsp;We select the direct carrier that will provide the most economical routing in an effort to maximize net revenues.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Revenues related to shipments where we act as an indirect carrier are reported based on the gross amount billed to the customer and include the charges for carrying the shipments. &nbsp;Based upon the terms in the contract of carriage, revenues are recognized at the time the freight is tendered to the direct carrier at origin. &nbsp;Costs related to the shipments are also recognized at this time.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>As an authorized cargo sales agent of most airlines and ocean shipping lines, we also arrange for transportation of individual shipments and receive a commission from the airline or ocean shipping line for arranging the shipments. &nbsp;When acting in this capacity, we do not consolidate shipments or have responsibility for shipments once they have been tendered to the carrier. &nbsp;Therefore, revenues include only the commissions and fees received. &nbsp;These revenues are recognized upon completion of the services.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Customs brokerage and other services</I>. &nbsp;Customs brokerage and import services involve providing services at destinations, such as helping customers clear shipments through customs by preparing required documentation, calculating and providing for payment of duties and other taxes on behalf of the customers as well as arranging for any required inspections by governmental agencies and arranging for delivery. &nbsp;We also offer a range of logistics services, distribution and materials management services, international insurance services, global project management services and trade facilitation services. &nbsp;Revenues include the fees received for these services and are recognized upon completion of the services.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Allowance for doubtful accounts</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Our allowance for doubtful accounts is determined using a combination of factors based on the expected ultimate recovery of trade receivables. &nbsp;We maintain a bad debt reserve for all customers based on a variety of factors, including the length of time receivables are past due, general and specific economic trends, significant one-time events and historical customer collection experience. &nbsp;Also, we record additional reserves for individual accounts when we become aware of a customer&#146;s inability to meet its financial obligations to us, such as in the case of bankruptcy filings or deterioration in the customer&#146;s operating results or financial position. &nbsp;Trade receivables include disbursements made by us on behalf of our customers for transportation costs and customs duties. &nbsp;As the billings to customers for these disbursements may be several times the amount of revenues and fees derived from these </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>44</P>
<P style="margin:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<HR style="padding-top:7.2pt; padding-bottom:7.2pt" noshade size=1.333>
<P style="page-break-before:never; margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>transactions, the inability to collect such amounts could result in losses greater than the revenues recognized when such billings were recorded. &nbsp;If circumstances related to customers change, our estimates of the allowance for doubtful accounts would be further adjusted.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Computer software</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Certain costs related to the development or purchase of internal-use software during the application development stage are capitalized and amortized over the estimated useful life of the software. &nbsp;The following types of costs incurred during the application development stage are capitalized: (i) external direct costs of materials and services consumed in developing or obtaining internal-use software, (ii) payroll and payroll related costs for employees who are directly associated with and who devote time to the internal-use software project, (iii) interest costs incurred in developing software for internal use, and (iv) costs to develop or obtain software that allows for access or conversion of old data into new systems. &nbsp;Costs related to the preliminary project stage, data conversion and the post-implementation/operation stage of a software development project are expensed as incurred. &nbsp;On retirement or sale of assets, the cost of such assets and accumulated depreciation are removed from the accounts and the gain or loss, if any, is credited or charged to income.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>We have incurred substantial costs during the periods presented related to a number of information systems projects that were being developed over that time period. &nbsp;Inherent in the capitalization of those projects are the assumptions that after considering the technological and business issues related to their development, such development efforts will be successfully completed and that benefits to be provided by the completed projects will exceed the costs capitalized to develop the systems. &nbsp;Management believes that all projects capitalized at December 31, 2005 will be successfully completed and will result in benefits recoverable in future periods.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><I>Goodwill and other intangibles</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>Goodwill represents the excess of purchase price over the fair value of net assets acquired. &nbsp;Goodwill is a residual amount and is determined after numerous estimates are made regarding the fair value of assets and liabilities included in a business combination, and therefore, indirectly affected by management&#146;s estimates and judgments. &nbsp;We review goodwill for impairment annually and whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate the carrying value of an asset may not be recoverable in accordance with SFAS No. 142, &#147;Goodwill and Other Intangible Assets.&#148; &nbsp;The provisions of SFAS No. 142 require that a two-step impairment test be performed on goodwill. &nbsp;In the first step, we compare the fair value of each reporting unit to its carrying value. &nbsp;We determine the fair value of our reporting units based on the present value of estimated future cash flows. &nbsp;If the fair value of the reporting unit exceeds the carrying value of the net assets assigned to that unit, goodwill is not impaired and we are not required to perform further testing. &nbsp;If the carrying value of the net assets assigned to the reporting unit exceeds the fair value of the reporting unit, then we must perform the second step in order to determine the implied fair value of the reporting unit&#146;s goodwill and compare it to the carrying value of the reporting unit&#146;s goodwill. &nbsp;If the carrying value of the reporting unit&#146;s goodwill exceeds its implied fair value, then we must record an impairment loss equal to the difference.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; text-indent:36pt; line-height:13pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify>The income approach, which we use to estimate the fair value of our reporting units is dependent on a number of factors including estimates of future market growth and trends; forecasted revenue, costs, cash flows and capital expenditures, and the timing thereof; appropriate discount rates; tax rates and other variables. &nbsp;We base our fair value estimates on assumptions we believe to be reasonable, but which are unpredictable and inherently uncertain. &nbsp;Actual future results may differ from those estimates. &nbsp;In addition, we make certain assumptions to allocate shared assets, liabilities and overhead costs to calculate the carrying values for each of our reporting units.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:11pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:11pt" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
